round1.title: Exactly One Passed
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take the marks of two students.

• Print "Yes" if EXACTLY ONE of them passed (pass mark is 40).
• Otherwise print "No".

Examples:

45 30  → Yes
45 80  → No
20 10  → No
40 39  → Yes
40 40  → No

Read the second example again before you start.

round1.title: Sorted or Not
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take three numbers.

• Print "Increasing" if each is strictly bigger than the one before.
• Print "Decreasing" if each is strictly smaller.
• Otherwise print "Not sorted".

Examples:

1 2 3    → Increasing
3 2 1    → Decreasing
1 3 2    → Not sorted
2 2 3    → Not sorted
5 5 5    → Not sorted

Strictly. Equal numbers are not increasing.

round1.title: Which Quadrant
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take x and y — a point on a graph.

Print which quadrant it is in:

• x positive, y positive → Quadrant 1
• x negative, y positive → Quadrant 2
• x negative, y negative → Quadrant 3
• x positive, y negative → Quadrant 4

But a point can also sit ON a line:

• On the x axis → "On X axis"
• On the y axis → "On Y axis"
• At (0, 0) → "Origin"

Examples:

3 4    → Quadrant 1
-3 -4  → Quadrant 3
0 5    → On Y axis
5 0    → On X axis
0 0    → Origin

round1.title: Right-Angled Triangle
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take three sides of a triangle.

• Print "Yes" if it is right-angled, "No" if not.

A triangle is right-angled when the squares of the two shorter sides add up to
the square of the longest one.

Examples:

3 4 5    → Yes
5 3 4    → Yes
4 5 3    → Yes
6 8 10   → Yes
2 3 4    → No
5 5 5    → No

Notice the first three. Same triangle, given in three different orders.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if a*a + b*b == c*c:   print("Yes")
elif a*a + c*c == b*b: print("Yes")
elif b*b + c*c == a*a: print("Yes")
else:                  print("No")

IN JAVASCRIPT: use === for the squares, a*a + b*b === c*c. Convert the sides
with Number() first — "3"*"3" happens to work because * coerces, but + does
not: "9" + "16" is "916", not 25. That single line is the most common JS bug
in this question.

TESTING: not assuming the input arrives in a helpful order. The longest side may
be any of the three, so all three arrangements have to be tried.

MARK WRONG IF:
- 5 3 4 or 4 5 3 prints "No" while 3 4 5 prints "Yes". They only tested
  a²+b²==c² and assumed the last one is the hypotenuse. THIS IS THE TRAP and
  most wrong answers are this exact one. Test 5 3 4 first.
- 5 5 5 prints "Yes".
- They sorted the three sides first and then tested once — that is CORRECT and
  rather elegant. Full marks, and say why it is good.

CHECK: 5 3 4, then 4 5 3, then 2 3 4.

round1.title: Do the Two Meetings Clash
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Two meetings on the same day. Take a start and end hour for each. The end is
always after the start.

• Print "Clash" if they overlap at all.
• Print "No clash" if they do not.

Meetings that only touch do NOT clash: 9–10 and 10–11 are fine.

Examples:

9 10  10 11   → No clash
9 11  10 12   → Clash
9 17  12 13   → Clash
12 13  9 17   → Clash
9 10  11 12   → No clash
14 15  9 10   → No clash

HINT: listing every way two meetings CAN overlap takes four cases and you will
miss one. There are only TWO ways they can miss each other. Find those instead.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if end1 <= start2:
    print("No clash")
else:
    if end2 <= start1: print("No clash")
    else:              print("Clash")

IN JAVASCRIPT: same shape with braces, and <= means the same thing. Convert the
four hours with Number() — comparing "9" and "10" as strings says 10 comes
first, which quietly inverts the answer.

TESTING: inverting the problem. This is the hardest question here and the only
one with a genuine insight in it — four ways to overlap, two ways to miss, so you
check for the misses.

MARK WRONG IF:
- 9 17 12 13 or 12 13 9 17 prints "No clash". They enumerated the overlap cases
  and missed "one meeting entirely inside the other". THE TRAP — test both, they
  fail in opposite directions.
- 9 10 10 11 prints "Clash". They used < where the question says touching is
  fine, so it needs <=.
- 14 15 9 10 prints "Clash". They assumed the first meeting always starts first.

CHECK: 9 17 12 13, then 12 13 9 17, then 9 10 10 11, then 14 15 9 10.

A student who found the two-misses shape rather than four overlap cases has done
the best thinking in the round. Tell them.

round1.title: Match Result
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

A team is chasing. Take the target (runs needed to win), the runs they have
scored, and the balls left.

• Reached the target → "Won"
• Balls still left → "Match still on"
• No balls left and one run short → "Tied"
• No balls left and further behind → "Lost"

Examples:

180  180  5    → Won
180  185  0    → Won
180  179  0    → Tied
180  150  0    → Lost
180  150  12   → Match still on
180  179  1    → Match still on

The order you check these in decides whether it works.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if runs >= target:
    print("Won")
else:
    if balls > 0:
        print("Match still on")
    else:
        if runs == target - 1: print("Tied")
        else:                  print("Lost")

IN JAVASCRIPT: same shape with braces. target - 1 works on numbers; if target
is still a string, "180" - 1 gives 179 (minus coerces) but "180" + 1 gives
"1801". Convert everything with Number() at the top and the whole class of bug
disappears.

TESTING: precedence between conditions that can both be true at once. Winning
off the last ball is both "reached the target" and "no balls left" — and only one
of those answers is right.

MARK WRONG IF:
- 180 185 0 prints "Lost" or "Tied". They checked balls == 0 before checking
  whether the target was reached. THE TRAP — test this one first.
- 180 179 1 prints "Tied". They checked the tie before the balls left.
- 180 179 0 prints "Lost" — they missed the tie, or used == target instead of
  target - 1.

CHECK: 180 185 0, then 180 179 1, then 180 179 0.

round1.title: Grade with a Plus
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take marks out of 100.

• 80 or more → A
• 60 to 79   → B
• 40 to 59   → C
• below 40   → F

Then: add a "+" if the LAST DIGIT of the marks is 5 or more.
An F never gets a plus.

Examples:

87   → A+
82   → A
79   → B+
71   → B
45   → C+
40   → C
35   → F
100  → A
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if marks < 40:
    print("F")
else:
    if marks >= 80:   g = "A"
    elif marks >= 60: g = "B"
    else:             g = "C"

    if marks % 10 >= 5: print(g + "+")
    else:               print(g)

IN JAVASCRIPT: the last digit is marks % 10 as well, and g + "+" concatenates
exactly as in Python. Convert marks with Number() first, or "87" % 10 works by
coercion while other comparisons do not.

TESTING: two INDEPENDENT rules. The letter comes from a range, the plus comes
from the last digit, and they have nothing to do with each other. Students who
try to write one branch per possible output end up with eight branches and a bug.

MARK WRONG IF:
- 35 prints "F+". The question says an F never gets a plus. THE TRAP.
- 100 prints "A+". Its last digit is 0.
- 79 prints "C+" — they mixed the letter bands up with the plus rule.
- Eight separate branches. It may work; it is the wrong shape. Show them the two
  independent steps.

CHECK: 35, 100, 79, 45.
